title: Startup Expert On Why You Don’t Need the Ivy League or 90-Hour Weeks to Win | Kofi Ampadu of a16z
guest: Kofi Ampadu, partner at Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) leading the Talent x Opportunity (TxO) initiative, former founder of beverage startup H2Melon
summary: Kofi Ampadu, a Ghanaian-American ex-consultant and two-time founder who now runs a16z's TxO program, talks about playing a rigged game and winning despite it, why founders' only responsibility is to do what they said they would do, and how he bootstrapped by moving into his sister's basement. He shares his daily 'win the day' tracking system (physical, mental, three tasks), a high-agency mindset for stress, and a rapid-fire true/false round on startup hot takes: 90-hour weeks, married co-founders, YC, Ivy League degrees, coding, white guys in hoodies, building in public and pitch decks.

ideas.idea: Know the rules of the game are rigged against you, decide to win despite it, build allies, and only try to change the rules once you have earned a bully pulpit.
ideas.detail: Founders of color are underfunded and everyone knows it, so complaining about the rules mid-game does no good; a rookie cannot rewrite league rules, but as you make progress you use your platform to change them. Kofi uses his hyphenated identity as an advantage and a chance to debunk stereotypes.

ideas.idea: A founder's responsibility is to do everything they said they would do, not to carry the weight of the next black or female founder getting funded.
ideas.detail: Founders lose trust when they promise XYZ and do ABC; if you execute your plan and it still fails, investors are astute enough to know most companies fail. Resilience is a double-edged sword because being too resilient compounds your opportunity cost.

ideas.idea: Do the thing now: the two most dangerous words are 'not now' because they become 'not ever'.
ideas.detail: A best friend sent Kofi a VC fund plan he had written in 2012 that overlaps about 85 percent with what he does today at TxO; he took roundabout paths through consulting looking for the perfect time. He also says you are rewarded for visibly trying and may get a shot sooner.

ideas.idea: The founder instinct shows up early as side hustles, and being a founder is the time you make the least money but are happiest because you have complete agency over every problem.
ideas.detail: In high school Kofi burned and sold mixtape CDs and charged underclassmen a delivery fee for off-campus lunch ('I invented DoorDash'). As an employee you often cannot solve the issue in front of you; as a founder you can hire, learn or fix it yourself.

ideas.idea: The real retirement goal is finding work you love enough to keep doing it at 70.
ideas.detail: Kofi's father, a former cab driver who opened a mom-and-pop shop, is nearly 70 and still working; when he described his typical day Kofi realized 'he's retired' because he loves it. Cherie cites Stanford professors teaching into their late 70s as the same role model.

ideas.idea: Being a VC is a learning cheat code because every founder meeting, even one you pass on, teaches you a new domain from someone living it daily.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: No two days are the same, you roll up your sleeves on portfolio problems, and TxO (started 2020, Kofi joined 2021) operates as a startup within the firm, so he still flexes entrepreneurial muscles without founder-level stress.

ideas.idea: Whenever you feel stressed, ask one foundational question: what can I do to change it? If nothing, stop stressing; if something, start small.
ideas.detail: Kofi says this protects his mental health, since stressing about something you cannot change only damages you; most actions that matter start small and minute.

ideas.idea: Anything worth having is hard now, easy later, so optimize for the long term.
ideas.detail: Going to the gym and waking early suck at first with no visible results; once results show, the habit becomes easy. Lasting change means accepting that things get harder in the short term.

ideas.idea: Going all in as a founder means cutting your own burn, even swallowing your pride to give up the nice apartment and move into your sister's basement.
ideas.detail: Kofi left a Manhattan apartment with a balcony to live in his sister's basement while bootstrapping, contributing groceries and free childcare; he argues you cannot claim the company needs money while paying rent you could redirect. Founders who raise should pay themselves the least, enough to live but not to save for vacations, because the payoff comes at the end.

ideas.idea: A supportive partner who does not second-guess your decisions is a cheat code, and a partner from an unrelated field gives you the 'regular person' perspective that breaks the tech echo chamber.
ideas.detail: Kofi's wife, a journalist, documentarian and photographer, shot product photos and helped with social posts for his startup; she is not a techno-optimist, so they debate rather than argue and she asks 'why do you need AI for that?'

ideas.idea: Hold 'brown bag lunches' with your partner where each researches a topic and pitches it to the other, who asks questions.
ideas.detail: Topics range from the societal benefits of AI to why francophone African countries peg their currency to the French system; the shared skill is that both journalists and investors must ask questions before committing resources. Cherie frames it as wanting a partner who is a lifelong learning partner (the 'zombie apocalypse standard': don't be bored with that person).

ideas.idea: Track whether you 'won the day' on three metrics (physical health, mental health, three daily tasks) rather than judging a year by New Year's resolutions.
ideas.detail: Started in 2020 after 2019 felt like a failure; Kofi logs daily in a spreadsheet with notes on bad weeks, posted weekly scores publicly on Twitter ('Week 1: won 6 of 7'), and reviews year over year to keep going up and to the right. Consultant motto: what doesn't get measured doesn't get tracked, and if you can't pinpoint why a week was bad you can't change it.

ideas.idea: Limit your daily to-do list to the three work things that matter, because we are always more ambitious than our abilities.
ideas.detail: A giant to-do list guarantees you finish nothing; after crossing off three, Kofi knows he had a good day, and usually gets more done anyway.

ideas.idea: Turn macro stress into a specific action within your expertise: during the BLM protests Kofi analyzed startup podcast guest lists and published 'Black Minds Matter' on TechCrunch.
ideas.detail: He found Black people were underrepresented as guests on prominent startup podcasts and argued that getting Black experts on product, engineering and investing onto those shows changes perception of a whole race; the hosts call this the ideal use of data and the bully pulpit.

ideas.idea: Make space for failure by time-blocking your wallowing: one day on the couch, then move forward.
ideas.detail: Expecting 100 percent happy days is a delusion; excuses are the cheapest thing to buy and spiraling is easy, but unless it is an extreme case like a job loss, a miss usually leaves you in the same spot you were in, so just reconfigure and continue.

ideas.idea: Failure is healthy: if you are not failing you are not trying hard enough, and aiming for perfection is why large companies never do anything worthwhile.
ideas.detail: Kids learning basketball are told to go faster; adults wait for the perfect moment. Kofi cites Adam Grant's finding that the best language learners start speaking on day one and embarrass themselves, which he is applying to learning French. Cherie admits she must be honest when scoring her days rather than stretching the metric.

ideas.idea: False that founders must work 90-hour weeks: building a company is a marathon run at a fast pace, with some 5-minute miles and some 7-minute miles.
ideas.detail: Hard work does not mean constant long hours; there will be 90-hour weeks but not always, and TxO tells founders at its retreat to take breaks.

ideas.idea: Dating or married co-founders are a flag but not a huge one; investors invest in risk and just need to ask the awkward questions to de-risk it.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: The risk is that a personal breakup takes the company down, so it has to be drilled into during diligence rather than dismissed.

ideas.idea: Y Combinator is not a scam; it has product-market fit because people would still apply if it took 5 percent and gave no money, thanks to its network of potential customers.
ideas.detail: A SaaS startup in YC can sell to every successful YC alumni company, so even just for traction and feedback the network is worth it.

ideas.idea: An Ivy League degree is not a prerequisite for founding a company; it signals intelligence but not everyone smart or talented went to one.
ideas.detail: This is the reason TxO exists: nobody has a right to build a company or raise money because of a college name, and talent is distributed beyond elite schools.

ideas.idea: You do not need to code to start a tech company, but you must bring something else that makes you valuable: selling, marketing, or recruiting the best talent.
ideas.detail: AI tools lower the coding bar; the danger is being the idea person whose only valuable asset is the engineer you hired.

ideas.idea: It is true, per the data, that raising money is easier for a white guy in a hoodie, but raising is hard for everyone because asking people for money is hard.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: Kofi frames it with radical empathy: even those with structural advantages experience fundraising as difficult.

ideas.idea: Building in public is not performative: it yields customer discovery, real-time feedback, and signals to investors how fast you move.
ideas.detail: If every post shows a founder jumping from B to F, investors want to get on that 'movement train'; the hosts note this validates their own build-in-public approach with Sisters Matcha.

ideas.idea: A pitch deck is the first move in an investor-founder relationship, so lying in it is a bad start and diligence will expose fake customer logos anyway.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: Kofi rejects the idea that most decks are well-designed lies; founders should put real care into them because the deck opens a long relationship.
